author: Dr. Michael Lee - Health Editor
title: Breaking News: Canadian Pancreatic Cancer Specialists Expect to Open Clinical Trials on Pill That Doubles Survival Time
text:
Key Clinical Takeaways: The experimental drug daraxonrasib demonstrated a doubling of survival time in pancreatic cancer patients during a U.S.-led study, prompting Canadian oncologists to initiate clinical trials. Dr. Jennifer Knox, a leading pancreatic cancer specialist, highlighted the drug’s potential to address “undruggable” molecular pathways in advanced pancreatic cancer. Regulatory pathways for daraxonrasib are accelerating, with trials expected to begin in Canadian centers by late 2026, pending Health Canada approvals. How Daraxonrasib Addresses a Persistent Clinical Challenge Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma remains one of the most lethal malignancies, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 10% for advanced stages. The pathogenesis of this disease is driven by mutations in KRAS, a protein that has historically proven resistant to targeted therapies. Daraxonrasib, an investigational small-molecule inhibitor, selectively targets KRAS G12C mutations through a novel mechanism of action, effectively disrupting downstream signaling pathways that fuel tumor proliferation and metastasis.
Canadian Pancreatic Cancer Specialists Expect According to the U.S.-led study published in Oncology News Central , the drug achieved a median overall survival of 14.2 months in patients with KRAS G12C-mutated pancreatic cancer, compared to 7.1 months with standard-of-care chemotherapy. These results represent a significant leap forward in a disease where therapeutic advances have been historically incremental.
Clinical Trial Design and Regulatory Pathways
The upcoming Canadian trials will follow a phased approach, beginning with a Phase II study to evaluate safety and efficacy in a broader patient cohort. Dr. Knox, medical director of the pancreatic cancer clinic at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto, emphasized the importance of replicating the U.S. Findings in diverse populations. “We need to ensure that the drug’s benefits are consistent across different genetic and environmental factors,” she stated in an interview with <a href="https://news.google.
